title: "Probability mass functions"

The [preceding page](discrete-random-variables.qmd) distinguished a random variable's declared codomain from its positive-probability support. Knowing that CMUdict phone count $X$ is discrete does not tell us how often its values occur. What object pairs each possible count with its probability?

We answer this question with the empirical distribution over the [CMUdict pronunciation entries introduced earlier](why-random-variables.qmd#the-pronunciation-entry-outcomes). Uniformly sampling one row gives each pronunciation entry the same mass; aggregating those row masses by `phone_count` produces an empirical probability mass function.

We construct that PMF from entry counts, check its nonnegative unit-sum requirements, and then use selected-value sums to distinguish zero probability from an impossible value.

```{r}
#| label: load-cmudict-pmf
library(ggplot2)

cmu <- read.csv(
  "data/cmudict/cmudict-pronunciations.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE,
  check.names = FALSE,
  na.strings = ""
)

phone_frequency <- as.data.frame(table(cmu$phone_count))
names(phone_frequency) <- c("phone_count", "entries")
phone_frequency$phone_count <-
  as.integer(as.character(phone_frequency$phone_count))
phone_frequency$mass <- phone_frequency$entries / nrow(cmu)

stopifnot(
  nrow(cmu) == 133854L,
  all(phone_frequency$mass >= 0),
  abs(sum(phone_frequency$mass) - 1) < 1e-12,
  sum(phone_frequency$entries) == nrow(cmu)
)

phone_frequency
```

The function assigning a probability to each codomain value is a [**probability mass function**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html), abbreviated [**PMF**](https://bruno.nicenboim.me/bayescogsci/ch-intro.html). We write

$$
p_X:\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\to[0,1],
\qquad
p_X(x)\equiv\mathbb{P}(X=x).
$$

For the empirical lexicon distribution with $N$ entries,

$$
\widehat p_X(x)
\equiv
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\mathbb 1\{X(\omega_i)=x\}.
$$

The capital $X$ denotes the random variable. The lowercase $x$ stands for one possible value.

For any particular count $x$, the table first computes
$n_x=\sum_i\mathbb 1\{X(\omega_i)=x\}$ and then divides by $N=133{,}854$.
Thus `entries` is $n_x$, `mass` is $n_x/N$, and the hat in
$\widehat p_X$ marks an empirical PMF over the pinned rows rather than an
unknown population PMF.

```{r}
#| label: cmudict-pmf-events
modal_row <- phone_frequency[which.max(phone_frequency$mass), ]
phone_threshold <- unname(quantile(cmu$phone_count, 0.75, type = 1))
upper_tail_mass <- sum(
  phone_frequency$mass[phone_frequency$phone_count > phone_threshold]
)

stopifnot(
  abs(modal_row$mass -
        mean(cmu$phone_count == modal_row$phone_count)) < 1e-12,
  abs(upper_tail_mass - mean(cmu$phone_count > phone_threshold)) < 1e-12
)

c(modal_phone_count = modal_row$phone_count,
  modal_mass = modal_row$mass,
  third_quartile = phone_threshold,
  mass_above_third_quartile = upper_tail_mass)
```

The most frequent value is `r modal_row$phone_count` phones, with mass `r sprintf("%.3f", modal_row$mass)`. By the PMF definition, this is the empirical probability of the event containing all pronunciation entries with that phone count.

## Checking the two PMF requirements

First, a PMF must assign nonnegative mass:

$$
p_X(x)\geq0
\qquad\text{for every }x\in\operatorname{cod}(X).
$$

Second, the masses across the codomain must sum to one:

$$
\sum_{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)}p_X(x)=1.
$$

Values in the codomain but outside the support contribute zero, so this sum has the same numerical value as a sum restricted to $\operatorname{supp}(X)$. The displayed assertions check nonnegativity and normalization from the data.

```{r}
#| label: plot-cmudict-pmf
#| fig-cap: "Empirical PMF of total phone count under uniform sampling from the pinned CMUdict pronunciation entries."
ggplot(phone_frequency, aes(phone_count, mass)) +
  geom_col(fill = "grey65", width = 0.8) +
  labs(x = "Phones in pronunciation", y = "Empirical probability") +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12)
```

## Adding mass across selected values

The probability that $X$ exceeds its empirical third quartile is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{P}(X>q_{.75})
&=\sum_{\substack{x\in\operatorname{cod}(X)\\x>q_{.75}}}p_X(x).
\end{aligned}
$$

Here $q_{.75}$ is `r phone_threshold` phones and the computed tail mass is `r sprintf("%.3f", upper_tail_mass)`. We add masses because exact-count events do not overlap.

This is the value-space version of [event
additivity](../foundations/probability-measures.qmd#the-three-requirements): the
preimages of distinct exact counts are disjoint outcome events, so their
probabilities add.

## Interpreting zero mass carefully

If $p_X(x)=0$, then $X=x$ has zero probability under the stated empirical model. This may mean only that the count does not occur in the pinned lexicon. It does not mean that no English pronunciation with that count can exist.

The PMF belongs to a represented sampling process. A lexicon weighted by pronunciation entries and a corpus weighted by word tokens would generally assign different masses to the same phone counts.

## Check your understanding

1. Use `phone_frequency` to compute $\mathbb{P}(X\leq q_{.75})$ and verify it by averaging a logical condition over `cmu$phone_count`.
2. Find an integer inside the observed minimum--maximum range that has zero mass. Does it belong to the declared codomain?
3. Recompute the PMF over unique `word` values after retaining only one pronunciation per word. Which probability experiment has changed?
4. Why would dropping rare counts and renormalizing define a conditional distribution rather than preserve the PMF above?
5. A student reads the modal bar height as the probability of an arbitrary
   English word token having that many phones. Which weighting has been lost?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The third quartile is 8 phones, and both the PMF sum and `mean(cmu$phone_count <= 8)` give $\mathbb{P}(X\leq q_{.75})=0.848693$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The integer 21 lies between the observed minimum and maximum but has mass zero; it still belongs to the declared nonnegative-integer codomain. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. Retaining one pronunciation for each of 133,228 unique words changes the experiment from sampling a pronunciation entry to sampling a word with one selected pronunciation. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. Dropping rare counts restricts the experiment to the event that the count was retained, and renormalization thus produces the conditional PMF given that event. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
5. The bar weights CMUdict pronunciation entries uniformly and contains no
   running-speech token frequencies, so it cannot describe an arbitrary corpus
   token without a new weighting model.

</details>

A PMF maps each declared value to a probability mass; empirically, that mass is
the value's row count divided by the common total. Probabilities add across
several discrete values because their preimages are disjoint. The [next
page](continuous-random-variables.qmd) considers a model whose values instead
fill an interval.
